name: Yindjibarndi
confidence_why: Wordick's 1982 reference grammar, the only first-hand description of Yindjibarndi, gives main stress on the first syllable with alternating secondary stresses and an optional pull of the main stress onto a long vowel in an even syllable, and the two later analyses built on his data, Kager 1992 and Stanton 2022, restate the same placement and differ only in how they formalize that optionality.

Now when a long vowel occurs in an even syllable, the basic pattern may not be adhered to ... If it is, then the stronger accent on the syllable, preceding it, will be attracted onto it. ... sweep_summary: Both works with stress in the title are the same chapter (Jacobs 2000, re-issued 2003 with a second DOI): 'The revenge of the uneven trochee' is an OT analysis of Latin main stress and shortening/syncope; I obtained the publisher's-version PDF (Radboud Repository hdl 2066/104107, green OA per Unpaywall/Semantic Scholar; the repository itself could not be reached by automated download, so it was downloaded from the 2019 Internet Archive copy; 21 pp., full text) and it contains no mention of Yindjibarndi, any Australian language, Wordick or Pama-Nyungan. Glottolog's attachment of ids 450864/453625 to yind1247 is a mis-tag; both items are irrelevant (other language: Latin), silent on the catalog, priority none. No new first-hand stress source for Yindjibarndi surfaced. The catalog's weight-hedged coding continues to rest on Wordick 1982 sec. 2.3.2 (pp. 41-42), which I re-read from the page scan and on-disk text this search of works with stress in the title: initial primary accent with alternating secondaries (1 3 2 3 2 3), a long vowel in an even syllable optionally/ordinarily attracting the stronger accent when pronounced long, rules explicitly 'not hard and fast' -- consistent with the catalog. Blocked routes noted in : degruyterbrill (bot challenge), repository.ubn.ru.

new_statements.reading: Primary accent on the first syllable with secondary accents on following odd syllables (1 3 2 3 2 3) whenever all vowels are short or long vowels sit only in odd syllables; a long vowel in an even syllable, if pronounced long, pulls the stronger accent off the preceding syllable onto itself (disyllables with long V2 'optionally' 3 1; trisyllables with long aa in syllable 2 'ordinarily' 3 1 2; high long vowels are usually broken into two shorts and keep 1 3 2 3), and Wordick adds that 'these rules are not hard and fast'. That is a weight-sensitive (long-vowel-attracting) system whose weight effect is optional/variable, which is exactly the catalog's 'weight-hedged' coding. Stanton 2022 (already held by the project, sec. 5.2 ex. 58) is secondary and restates Wordick pp. 41-42.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog's deciding source (Wordick 1982:41-42, quoted in existing_statements): initial main stress with alternating secondaries when all vowels are short, and attraction of the stress onto a long vowel in an even syllable. Kager adds a formal analysis (moraic trochees built left to right, End Rule Left, clash avoidance on both mora and syllable layers, final degenerate feet allowed) and restates the weight effect as a categorical surface ban on unstressed heavy syllables, with the variability Wordick reported ('optionally', 'ordinarily', 'not hard and fast') relocated to a choice between long-vowel breaking and light-syllable skipping. All data are Wordick's; no indepe…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Main stress is on the first syllable by default (left-to-right trochees, End Rule Left), with alternating secondary stress on following odd syllables (wílarrà, pángkarrìi, pámrturràrna, ngúnhungkìiri). A long-vowelled (heavy) syllable is never left unstressed: when a light initial syllable is followed by a heavy one, the light syllable is skipped and main stress falls on the heavy second syllable (tyarráarn 'frog', purnngáarri 'cyclonic cloud', ngurnáapurràa); alternatively a long high vowel in an even syllable is broken into two short syllables and the default initial pattern applies (pírri.ì ~ pirríi, páli.ìrri ~ palíirri, káayu.ùrru). Kager treats the surface ban on weak heavy syllables as categorical ('these never surface in weak positions') and models it with moraic trochees plus clash avoidance on both the mora and syllable layers.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: binary alternation from left to right on the mora layer (moraic trochees), heavy syllables always foot heads; final degenerate feet allowed, so odd-numbered final syllables carry a secondary stress (wílarrà, káarrwarà, mártu.urràa); a light syllable before a heavy one is skipped so that the heavy syllable gets the stress; two adjacent long vowels force breaking of the second (máapu.ù, káayu.ùrru, máapu.urràa).
new_statements.exceptions: Breaking 'competes or alternates' with light-syllable skipping in light-heavy sequences (26k, m, o: pírri.ì or pirríi; páli.ìrri or palíirri); breaking is obligatory in heavy-heavy sequences; one 'isolated example' of a non-high long vowel in an even syllable with a double-heavy foot, páarnpaarn 'mulga parrot' (26h), called 'marginally attested' in (27d). On p. 307 Kager cites 'Wordick (1980, 17-18)' although only Wordick 1982 is in his references (apparent typo).
new_statements.identity_note: Kager describes Yindjibarndi solely from Wordick 1982 (Pacific Linguistics C-71); no dialect is named beyond Wordick's description. The two other Australian languages treated in the paper (Guugu Yimidhirr, sec. 6; Pintupi, sec. 1) and Finnish/Estonian are not about this language.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on placement. The only nuance: Wordick 1982 (the catalog's deciding source) frames the attraction of stress onto an even-syllable long vowel as optional/ordinary ('these rules are not hard and fast'), whereas Kager 1992 formalizes the ban on unstressed heavy syllables as categorical at the surface and puts the variation in the alternation between long-vowel breaking (pírri.ì) and light-syllable skipping (pirríi). Both agree that with only short vowels the pattern is initial main stress plus alternating secondaries, and both agree on the same example words. Kager's single anomalous form páarnpaarn 'mulga parrot' (a long vowel left in a weak position) is also in Wordick.

audit.reasoning: The classification (weight-hedged: default initial primary with alternating secondaries; a long vowel in the second syllable, if realised long, attracts primary, optionally in disyllables and 'ordinarily' with aa in trisyllables; high long vowels usually broken; final consonants weightless) rests on Wordick 1982 sec. 2.3.2, the sole reference grammar of the language, and the deciding quotation is verbatim at the stated pages in the PDF we hold/text/page scan.
